scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Following the introduction of the foxtrot around 1914, two tempo variations emerged: a slow foxtrot performed at approximately forty measures per minute and a fast version executed at over fifty measures per minute.

In the United States, the fast version took the name Peabody, named after Lieutenant William Frank Peabody (1873–1939), a New York police officer and popular ragtime dancer who favored high-tempo foxtrots around 1915.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally danced in ragtime social dance halls in 1910s and 1920s New York, the Peabody developed into a competitive ballroom category and exhibition feature.
It represents a playful, energetic expression of early American ragtime dance culture.
Today it is a revived tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The Peabody is a brisk dance that covers expansive floor space.
Performed to 2/4 or 4/4 ragtime music, it operates essentially as a fast one-step featuring long, gliding strides and occasional syncopations.
Dancers utilize an unusual English or right-outside position where the leader holds the partner on his right side.
Watch for Right-Outside Glide, Leader Side-Change Promenade, Peabody Upper-Body Dip.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (_VOFkpsxuv0)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Progressive partner travel covering large areas of the ballroom floor.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Danced to 2/4 or 4/4 ragtime and early New Orleans jazz compositions played at fast tempos.

Typical music includes pieces such as 'When the Saints Go Marching In,' 'Ain't She Sweet?,' 'Yes, We Have No Bananas,' 'Tiger Rag,' and 'Bourbon Street Parade.' Big band and mid-century tunes with suitable tempo, such as Glen Gray's 'Maniac's Ball' and Pat Ballard's 'Mr. Sandman,' are also used.
Listen for the Piano, Brass, Reeds, Drums.
The pulse is 2/4 or 4/4 at about 110 beats a minute.
A high-tempo ragtime or New Orleans jazz ensemble featuring fast, syncopated brass and piano drive that propels continuous rapid gliding movement.

narration: In exhibitions and competitions, dancers frequently wear period ragtime clothing.
Gentlemen wear suits accompanied by bowler hats or straw boaters, while ladies wear long, full dresses.
The setting is traditionally a ballroom floor allowing continuous travel along the line of dance.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Lieutenant William Frank Peabody (1873–1939), the New York police officer after whom the dance was named; exhibition dancers Tony DeMarco and Sally DeMarco; film performers Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers; competitive and demonstration dancers Sandra Cameron, Paul Grecki, Chad Fasca, Midori Asakura, Mark Judkins, and Brenda Judkins.
Evolved from the fast foxtrot during the ragtime era of the 1910s and 1920s in New York City.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Peabody is parent of Foxtrot: The Peabody evolved from the fast variation of the foxtrot introduced around 1914.
Peabody is child of Quickstep: English dancers attempted to reconstruct the Peabody, giving rise to International Quickstep.
Peabody is influence of Charleston: Exhibition dancers frequently blend Charleston figures into energetic Peabody performances.

scenes.title: Step A — slowly
narration: Step 1: Adopt the right-outside (English) partner position.
Step 2: Initiate forward progress with long, smooth, gliding strides around the room.
Footwork from the sources: Long, smooth gliding strides with occasional syncopations and quick directional changes.

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer
narration: Step 3: Execute simple promenade walks while maintaining right-side alignment.
Step 4: Incorporate simple left and right turns along the floor pattern.
Drill: Execute continuous forward gliding steps to a moderate 2/4 rhythm.

scenes.title: Put it together
narration: Step A, then Step B, without stopping. Slow first.
Now half tempo. Now full tempo.
Mirror: the instructor faces you and mirrors, so your right is your right.
Drill: Maintain frame consistency while traveling counterclockwise along the floor boundary.
